prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated exceptional reasoning capabilities in open-loop autonomous driving tasks, such as scene understanding and risk assessment. However, these systems fundamentally lack the capability to execute **closed-loop vehicle control**. Existing approaches typically rely on open-loop paradigms that lack feedback mechanisms, making them brittle against real-world disturbances. Furthermore, when adapting these models for end-to-end control using standard behavior cloning, they suffer from the **distribution shift (or "drifting") problem**: small errors accumulate over time, leading the vehicle into unfamiliar states from which it cannot recover, as the training data only covers expert, error-free trajectories.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that MLLMs can be effectively adapted for robust, closed-loop autonomous driving by shifting from text generation to direct decision regression and utilizing **online imitation learning** via a privileged expert system.

Specifically, we posit that:
1.  Replacing standard auto-regressive text decoding with specialized **numerical decision heads** will enable the speed and precision required for real-time control.
2.  We can mitigate the "drifting" issue by training a vision-based Student Agent under the supervision of a **Privileged Expert LLM**—one that has access to ground-truth simulation state data. By allowing the Expert to intervene and correct the Student during training, we can aggregate a dataset that teaches the model how to recover from mistakes.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose an end-to-end architecture that processes multi-view visual data and vehicle states to output low-level control signals. The approach consists of three key components:

### 1. Multi-View Visual Tokenization
To perceive the environment comprehensively, we will design a **Multi-View Visual Tokenizer**. Instead of processing a single front-view image, this module will ingest images from multiple camera angles (e.g., front-left, front, front-right) to cover a wider field of view. These images will be encoded via visual encoders and projected into the LLM's text embedding space, allowing the language model to "see" the panoramic context while maintaining critical visual details.

### 2. Decision Heads (DeciHeads) for Direct Control
Standard LLMs output text tokens from a vast vocabulary, which is inefficient and imprecise for continuous control. We propose to modify the output layer of the MLLM. Instead of predicting next-token probabilities over a vocabulary, the model will use specific tokens to trigger **Decision Heads (MLPs)**. These heads will directly regress numerical driving decisions, specifically:
*   **Target Speed and Angle:** High-level commands to be executed by PID controllers.
*   **Waypoints and Route Points:** Trajectory predictions used for auxiliary supervision and guidance.

### 3. Online Imitation Learning with a Privileged Expert
To solve the error accumulation problem, we will implement a two-stage training strategy inspired by the **DAgger (Dataset Aggregation)** algorithm:
*   **The Expert (Teacher):** We will instantiate a duplicate MLLM architecture that receives **privileged information** (direct access to ground-truth object locations and map data) rather than just raw pixels. This allows the Expert to make near-perfect decisions.
*   **The Agent (Student):** The deployment model, which sees only camera images.
*   **On-Policy Supervision:** During the second training stage, the Student drives the vehicle. The Expert monitors the Student's planned decisions in real-time. If the Student's prediction deviates significantly from the Expert's, the Expert takes control to prevent failure and records the corrective action. This interaction generates a dataset of "corrective" examples, which is used to fine-tune the Student, effectively teaching it how to recover from its own errors.

## Expected Contribution
We expect this research to bridge the gap between high-level LLM reasoning and low-level reactive control. By successfully implementing a closed-loop system with online imitation learning, we aim to demonstrate that MLLMs can serve as reliable end-to-end drivers that do not merely analyze scenes passively but actively navigate and recover from disturbances. Additionally, the introduction of "Decision Heads" will provide a blueprint for making Large Language Models computationally efficient enough for real-time robotic control tasks.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of an end-to-end closed-loop autonomous driving system utilizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). The experiments were designed to test the efficacy of a multi-view visual tokenizer, specific decision heads, and an expert-guided online imitation learning strategy.

### Datasets and Environment
*   **Simulator:** CARLA Simulator.
*   **Data Collection Strategy:** Two-stage process.
    *   **Stage 1 (Behavior Cloning):** We utilized a rule-based autopilot to collect data across CARLA Towns 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 10. The dataset covered various weather, lighting, and daytime conditions. Data was collected at 2 Hz. After filtering for correctness (removing stuck instances), the dataset comprised **300,000 samples**.
    *   **Stage 2 (DAgger / Online Imitation):** The agent ran on selected training scenarios/routes. An expert model (with privileged access to objects within 30m) provided on-policy supervision. If the agent-expert discrepancy exceeded a threshold, the expert took control and recorded data. This resulted in approximately **150,000 aggregated samples**.
*   **Inputs:**
    *   **Visual:** Three front-view cameras (Front-Left, Front, Front-Right) at resolution **384 x 384**.
    *   **Text:** Current vehicle speed and target point.
*   **Outputs (Predicted):**
    *   Target Speed (used for longitudinal PID control).
    *   Target Angle (used for lateral PID control).
    *   Waypoints (8 points representing vehicle position 4 seconds into the future).
    *   Route Points (10 points evenly sampled from the global route).

### Evaluation Metrics
We evaluated performance on the **CARLA Longest6 Benchmark** (36 extended routes).
*   **Main Metrics:**
    *   **Driving Score (DS):** Product of RC and IS.
    *   **Route Completion (RC):** Percentage of route completed.
    *   **Infraction Score (IS):** Geometric series of penalty factors.
*   **Infraction/Exception Counts:**
    *   Pedestrian collision (Ped)
    *   Vehicle collision (Veh)
    *   Static object collision (Stat)
    *   Red light violation (Red)
    *   Route deviations (Dev)
    *   Scenario time out (TO)
    *   Agent block (Block)

### Baselines Compared
We compared our method against the following prior works:
*   **WOR:** Uses commands instead of target points.
*   **LAV (v1 & v2):** Predicts waypoints refined through a GRU.
*   **TransFuser:** Transformer-based sensor fusion (Camera + LiDAR).
*   **Perception PlanT:** Object-level input representation.
*   **InterFuser:** Predicts density maps and traffic rule flags.
*   **Transfuser++:** State-of-the-art method fusing point clouds and images; tested with and without triple data augmentation.
*   **LMDrive:** End-to-end vehicle control using Vicuna-7B (Open-loop focus previously, tested here in closed-loop).

### Implementation Details
*   **Model Architecture:**
    *   **Planner:** Tiny-scale LLMs (Qwen-0.5B and TinyLLaMA) fine-tuned for multimodal understanding.
    *   **Visual Encoder:** SigLIP (384 x 384).
    *   **Decision Heads (DeciHeads):** Four MLP heads replacing the vocabulary output, treating decision variables as regression tasks.
*   **Training Configuration:**
    *   **Hardware:** 16 NVIDIA A800 GPUs.
    *   **Training Time:** Approximately 75 hours.
    *   **Epochs:** 60.
    *   **Learning Rate:** 2e-5 with a cosine annealing schedule.
    *   **Precision:** FP16.
    *   **Strategy:** Fully fine-tuned end-to-end (excluding the visual encoder).
*   **Inference Hardware:** Single NVIDIA A800 GPU.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

### Model Architecture and Design
*   **Observation:** The Multi-View Visual Tokenizer (MV-VT) utilizing three front views (left, center, right) ensured comprehensive coverage of the vehicle's frontal and lateral views. We noted that back-view images had limited utility in CARLA benchmarks and were excluded to maintain efficiency.
*   **Observation:** The specific design of the visual tokenizer allowed us to maintain a sufficient perception range without compromising image details, avoiding information loss associated with resizing single large-scope images.
*   **Observation:** The use of dedicated "Decision Heads" (DeciHeads) allowed the model to predict numerical values (Target Speed, Angle, Waypoints) using only four tokens per prediction cycle. This provided a significant speed increase over text-based output representations, which would have required approximately 160 tokens.

### Training Dynamics and Supervision
*   **Observation:** We observed that LMDrive, which converts multimodal data to BEV and then projects to text, failed to achieve satisfactory performance (DS 36) in closed-loop settings, likely due to the lack of high-quality pretrained multimodal LLMs for BEV data.
*   **Observation:** Training from scratch without LLM visual pretraining slowed down convergence and degraded final results (DS dropped from 60 to 47 in ablations).
*   **Observation:** The inclusion of Waypoints and Route Points as auxiliary supervision tasks improved the model's ability to perceive the target route and anticipate future actions, even though they were not used for direct control.
*   **Observation:** Relying solely on behavior cloning (Stage 1) led to error accumulation. The introduction of the Expert model with privileged information (Stage 2 DAgger) significantly improved robustness, raising the Driving Score from 63 to 70.

### Control and Efficiency
*   **Observation:** Using predicted Waypoints or Route Points to derive control signals (via PID) resulted in noisy and unstable control, leading to inferior performance compared to directly predicting Target Speed and Target Angle.
*   **Observation:** Scaling the LLM backbone from 0.5B to 8B parameters did not yield a proportional performance gain (DS 63 vs 65) but reduced inference speed drastically (from 8.1 FPS to 0.4 FPS), making large models impractical for real-time deployment.
*   **Observation:** The final model (DriveGPT4-V2) achieved State-of-the-Art performance (DS 70) on the CARLA Longest6 benchmark, outperforming the previous best method (Transfuser++) which scored 65 DS. It specifically excelled in reducing collision rates and red light violations compared to baselines.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```


```latex
  \end{subfigure}

  \label{fig:short}

```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The current landscape of autonomous driving (AD) systems is bifurcated into two limited approaches. Traditional systems rely heavily on rule-based decision-making modules; while interpretable, these lack adaptability to the infinite variability of real-world scenarios. Conversely, recent learning-based approaches, specifically those leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), have shown promise in reasoning and scene understanding. However, existing MLLM-based driving systems are predominantly **open-loop**. They lack real-time feedback mechanisms, rendering them susceptible to "drifting"—a phenomenon where minor errors accumulate over time, leading the vehicle into unsafe states (e.g., collisions or path deviations). Furthermore, standard imitation learning methods like behavior cloning (BC) fail to correct these accumulating errors because the agent never experiences (and thus never learns to recover from) the states induced by its own mistakes. Additionally, current MLLM architectures rely on textual token output for control, which is computationally inefficient and lacks the numerical precision required for smooth vehicle dynamics.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **DriveGPT4-V2**, an end-to-end, closed-loop autonomous driving system that harnesses the reasoning capabilities of LLMs while addressing the stability issues of open-loop systems.

Our core hypothesis consists of three pillars:
1.  **Architecture Efficiency:** We hypothesize that by replacing standard textual output heads with specialized **Decision Heads (DeciHeads)**, we can directly regress numerical control variables using single tokens, significantly improving inference speed and control precision.
2.  **Perception Coverage:** We propose a **Multi-View Visual Tokenizer (MV-VT)** that processes inputs from multiple front-facing cameras, ensuring a comprehensive field of view required for safe planning while maintaining visual detail.
3.  **Online Robustness (Expert-in-the-Loop):** We posit that training cannot rely solely on offline behavior cloning. Instead, we will implement an **online imitation learning** framework where a "privileged" Expert LLM (with access to ground-truth state data) provides on-policy supervision to the Agent LLM. This will allow the agent to learn recovery behaviors and mitigate error accumulation in closed-loop operation.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a multimodal end-to-end architecture that maps sensor inputs directly to vehicle control decisions.

### 1. Model Architecture
The system, denoted as DriveGPT4-V2, will utilize a tiny-scale LLM (e.g., Qwen-0.5B or TinyLLaMA) as the reasoning backbone to ensure real-time inference capabilities.

#### A. Multimodal Input and Tokenization
The model will accept two modalities:
*   **Visual Input:** Three front-view camera images (Front-Left, Front-Center, Front-Right), each resized to $384 \times 384$. This multi-view setup ensures coverage of lateral traffic and potential collision risks.
*   **Text Input:** The vehicle's current state (current speed) and navigation instruction (target point).

**Multi-View Visual Tokenizer (MV-VT):**
We will employ a pretrained visual encoder (specifically SigLIP) to extract feature patches from the three input images. Unlike standard approaches that might crop or excessively resize a single wide image, we will process the three views independently to preserve detail. These feature patches will be mapped into the LLM's text embedding domain via a trained projection layer.

#### B. Output Representations and Decision Heads
Standard LLMs output text tokens (e.g., generating the text "1.5" requires multiple tokens). To optimize for driving, we will replace the vocabulary output head with four specific **Decision Heads (DeciHeads)**. These are Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) designed to predict numerical values directly.

The LLM will be trained to output four specific latent tokens, each corresponding to one of the following heads:
1.  **Target Speed ($TS$):** The desired longitudinal velocity.
2.  **Target Angle ($TA$):** The desired steering angle.
3.  **Waypoints ($WP$):** A sequence of 8 future $x,y$ coordinates representing the trajectory over the next 4 seconds.
4.  **Route Points ($RP$):** A sequence of 10 points sampled evenly from the global route ahead to guide high-level planning.

**Control Logic:**
While the model predicts trajectory points ($WP$ and $RP$) for supervision and scene understanding, the actual vehicle control will be derived from $TS$ and $TA$. We will implement two PID controllers:
*   **Speed PID:** Adjusts throttle and brake based on the predicted $TS$ and current vehicle speed.
*   **Steering PID:** Adjusts the steering wheel based on the predicted $TA$.

### 2. Online Imitation Learning Strategy
To solve the closed-loop drift issue, we will employ a two-stage training process involving a Privileged Expert.

**The Expert Model ($M_E$):**
We will construct an Expert LLM that shares the same architecture as the Agent ($M_A$) but receives **privileged information** inputs. This includes ground-truth text descriptions of surrounding objects (vehicles, pedestrians), traffic light states, and hazard information. This allows $M_E$ to act as a highly reliable supervisor.

**Stage 1: Behavior Cloning (BC)**
We will first train both $M_A$ and $M_E$ using offline data collected by a rule-based autopilot. The inputs will be sensor data, and the labels will be the autopilot's decisions.

**Stage 2: DAgger with On-Policy Supervision**
We will implement an online imitation learning loop inspired by the DAgger (Dataset Aggregation) algorithm.
1.  The Agent $M_A$ controls the vehicle in the simulation.
2.  Simultaneously, the Expert $M_E$ observes the state and predicts its own optimal actions.
3.  We calculate the discrepancy between the Agent and Expert predictions.
4.  **Intervention:** If the discrepancy exceeds a predefined threshold, the Expert $M_E$ takes over control of the vehicle to prevent safety violations (exceptions).
5.  **Aggregation:** The data sample at the moment of intervention (and subsequent frames) is recorded with the Expert's output as the ground truth label.
6.  The Agent is fine-tuned on this aggregated dataset, effectively learning to handle the specific "edge cases" that previously caused it to fail.

### 3. Mathematical Formulation and Loss Function
We will formulate the training objective as a regression task using the L1 loss. We define the loss components for the four Decision Heads:
*   $\mathcal{L}_{TS}$: Loss for Target Speed.
*   $\mathcal{L}_{TA}$: Loss for Target Angle.
*   $\mathcal{L}_{WP}$: Loss for Waypoints (average L1 distance across 8 points).
*   $\mathcal{L}_{RP}$: Loss for Route Points (average L1 distance across 10 points).

The total loss function $\mathcal{L}$ is defined as:
$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{TS} + \mathcal{L}_{TA} + \mathcal{L}_{WP} + \mathcal{L}_{RP} $$

By minimizing this objective, we optimize the model to produce precise numerical values for vehicle dynamics and trajectory planning simultaneously.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Framework for Closed-Loop MLLM Driving:** We expect to demonstrate that MLLMs can be successfully adapted from open-loop QA tasks to closed-loop control by integrating online imitation learning, bridging the gap between reasoning and real-time actuation.
2.  **Enhanced Robustness via Privileged Expert:** We anticipate that the Expert-in-the-Loop training strategy will significantly reduce infraction rates (collisions, lane deviations) compared to standard behavior cloning by exposing the agent to corrective feedback distribution.
3.  **Optimized Inference Efficiency:** The introduction of DeciHeads and the MV-VT architecture is expected to provide a theoretical basis for high-frequency inference suitable for real-world deployment, eliminating the latency overhead associated with auto-regressive text generation for numerical control.

notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
